title: How to turn dictation into polished legal drafts on Mac in 2026
metaTitle: Turn dictation into polished legal drafts on Mac: 2026 guide
description: Raw dictation reads like a rough draft. Here is how lawyers on Mac clean it up with settings, a review routine and voice help.
targetKeyword: turn dictation into polished legal drafts
intro: To turn dictation into polished legal drafts on a Mac, clean the text in three passes: set up dictation first, fix the flagged words, then read the draft the way a reviewer would. Raw dictation looks finished, but it hides errors that matter in a contract or a demand letter. This page covers what the mess costs you, why it happens, free fixes you can start today, and where Lazur helps.
tldr: Set up dictation before you speak, including punctuation and your list of names and defined terms.
Fix the blue underlined words, then check names, dates, numbers and negatives against the file.
Read for meaning after the facts check out, then read the whole draft aloud once.
Faster speech does not mean cleaner text. Studies show errors still slip through.
Follow your firm's rules on client data before you dictate any matter details.

blocks.text: Dictation feels finished the moment you stop talking. The text on screen looks tidy, and the sentences sound like yours. That is the trap. Speech recognition gets most words right, then drops small things that matter in a contract. A missing 'not' flips a clause. A party name that sounds right can still be wrong.
Dictation cleanup for lawyers: what it costs you

The cost is not only minutes. It is the second read you must take, and that read gets harder when a draft looks smooth. Clinical research shows the pattern. In a JAMA Network Open study of 217 dictated clinical notes from 144 physicians, speech-recognition drafts carried a 7.4% error rate. Transcriptionist review cut that to 0.4%, and signed notes reached 0.3%. The data is from 2016 and covers doctors, not lawyers, so read it as a pattern rather than a legal benchmark.

rows: A second pair of eyes cut errors sharply
Final sign-off removed most of what was left

blocks.text: Speed brings its own trade. An arXiv paper by Ruan et al. found speech entry 2.93 times faster than keyboard for English, at 153 words per minute against 52. Final text still had more uncorrected errors from speech, at 1.30% against 0.79% for keyboard. That test used short phrases typed on phones, not legal drafts. The lesson still holds. Faster input does not mean cleaner output.

Time pressure makes it worse. A 2026 ABA and Krill Strategies study of nearly 37,000 lawyers found that 47.4% screened positive for high burnout. Another 27% had considered leaving the profession because of mental health, burnout or stress. The study did not measure dictation. It does show why you should protect your review time instead of rushing past it.
Why raw dictation comes out messy

Three things cause most of the mess. The recognizer hears sounds and guesses words. It adds punctuation where you did not mean to pause. It also has no idea that 'the Lessee' is a defined term or that a case name needs italics. Each guess is small. Together they make a draft that looks clean and reads wrong.
Set up Mac dictation before you speak

Start in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Apple's help page says auto-punctuation can be turned off there. If you dictate punctuation on purpose, turn it off, so the tool does not add commas you did not mean. If you rely on the tool's punctuation, leave it on and check every mark during review.

items: Write a short list of party names, judges, courts and defined terms in a plain note.
Add the same names to your personal dictionary in Lazur, if you use it.
Store standard clauses as snippets, so you can drop them in by voice.
Use a headset mic in a quiet room. Background noise makes recognition harder.
Dictate one test paragraph and read it back before you start the real draft.

blocks.text: How to clean up a dictated legal draft step by step

items: Read the whole draft once without editing. Mark only the spots that stop you.
Click each blue underlined word in Apple Dictation text and pick the right alternative. Apple's help page describes this.
Check every name, judge, court and date against the matter file. Search for each one.
Search for each defined term, such as 'the Lessee', and confirm it matches the definition.
Re-read numbers, dates and negatives. Read each clause that says 'not', 'no' or 'unless' twice.
Turn on Track Changes in Word before you edit, so a reviewer sees each change.
Read the final draft aloud once. Your ear catches run-ons and dropped words your eyes skip.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. You dictate a demand letter and say 'shall not' to describe a duty. The text reads 'shall.' The sentence still looks fine, so a quick read misses it. Your negative check catches it. A similar problem happens with names. The recognizer writes a name that sounds right but is not in the file. A search against the matter file catches that one.
Mistakes that make cleanup worse

items: Editing while you dictate. Stop, read back the sentence, then continue.
Fixing one paragraph at a time without reading the whole draft. Context can change meaning.
Trusting the tool's punctuation in a clause with several conditions.
Pasting client text into an unapproved AI tool to polish it, before checking your firm's policy.
Skipping the final read because the draft looks professional.

blocks.text: Dictation tools for Mac lawyers compared

Several tools handle dictation on a Mac. Apple's built-in Dictation is the starting point for most people. Microsoft's Dictate feature in Word for Mac starts with ⌥F1, and it needs a Microsoft 365 subscription and sign-in. Superwhisper runs on Mac and offers custom vocabulary. Wispr Flow removes filler words and handles mid-sentence corrections. Dragon Professional 16 lists only Windows, so do not plan a Mac workflow around it.

blocks.text: Where Lazur fits in the cleanup routine

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Its personal dictionary and snippets help with names and standard clauses. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

Ask Lazur to walk you through a setting when the path is hard to find. It guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. For review, hold ⌥⌘ over a paragraph and ask what it says. Treat the answer as a reading aid. Check it against the source yourself.
Client data and firm AI rules come first

blocks.title: Check your firm's rules first
blocks.text: Client names, matter facts and privileged details may be restricted by your employer. Follow your firm's policy before you dictate or paste client material into any tool. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Read its privacy notes, then ask your firm before using it on a live matter.
Regulated work calls for extra care. Lawyers, nurses and accountants answer to rules on client and patient data. Your employer sets what is allowed, not this guide.
What to do next with a live draft

Pick one draft that is not urgent. Run the three passes and log each error you catch. After a week, you will know which habits help. For Word-specific steps, read [Word for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/word) or [AI assistant for Word on Mac](/apps/word). If you want a rough accuracy check first, try the [dictation accuracy checker](/tools/dictation-accuracy-checker).

faq.question: Can I turn dictation into a polished legal draft without a paid tool?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple Dictation is built into macOS, and you can clean its output with a review routine. Paid tools can save typing, but they do not replace your read. Check every name, date and negative yourself.

faq.question: What do the blue underlined words mean in Apple Dictation?
faq.answer: Apple's help page says uncertain words are underlined in blue. Click the word to choose an alternative. If the right word is not offered, retype it, then add the term to your matter list for the next draft.

faq.question: Should I turn off auto-punctuation for legal dictation?
faq.answer: Turn it off in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation if you prefer to dictate marks yourself. Leave it on if the tool's marks save you more time than they cost. Either way, check every comma in a clause with several conditions.

faq.question: Does Word Dictate work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft's Dictate page lists Mac for Word and says it starts with ⌥F1. It requires a Microsoft 365 subscription and sign-in. Check your firm's licensing before you rely on it for client documents.

faq.question: Is Dragon a good choice for a Mac?
faq.answer: The Dragon Professional 16 release notes list only Windows operating systems and no macOS support. Check the current product page before you buy anything, because versions change.

faq.question: Can Lazur write the final draft for me?
faq.answer: Lazur drafts and types text, and it can help you reword a paragraph. It does not know your facts, your jurisdiction or your firm's style unless you tell it. You review and approve every line before it goes into a matter.

faq.question: Is client information safe when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's policy still decides what you may share.

costs.title: Time you spend on a second read
costs.text: Every dictated draft needs a second read. That read takes longer when errors hide inside sentences that look fine. You pay for the time in evenings or billable hours. You also pay in the rework that follows when a reviewer finds a problem late.

costs.title: Errors that look right
costs.text: Speech recognition often picks a plausible word, not an obviously wrong one. A name that sounds right passes a quick glance. So does 'shall' for 'shall not'. In the JAMA study, drafts carried a 7.4% error rate until a human review step brought it to 0.4%.

costs.title: Speed that hides mistakes
costs.text: Speech can beat typing on speed. The Ruan et al. study found speech 2.93 times faster than keyboard for English. Final text still had more uncorrected errors from speech, at 1.30% against 0.79%. That test used short phrases on phones, so it does not prove the same for a legal draft. It does show that quick input and clean output are different goals.

costs.title: Pressure on the person doing the review
costs.text: Lawyers already carry heavy loads. The 2026 ABA and Krill Strategies study found that 47.4% of nearly 37,000 lawyers screened positive for high burnout. A tired reader is more likely to skim. Build review time into your plan, so the second read does not get cut when the week gets busy.

costs.title: Client trust and firm risk
costs.text: A visible error in a letter to a client or to opposing counsel damages trust. A flipped negative in a clause can cause real harm. If cleanup happens in a tool your firm has not approved, you may also break internal rules on client data. Check before you paste.

causes.title: The recognizer guesses words
causes.text: Speech recognition turns sound into likely words. It does not know your matter. When the audio is unclear, it picks the most common match, which may be a near miss. You only see the near miss if you read closely, and a quick scan will not show it.

causes.title: Punctuation is guessed
causes.text: Auto-punctuation adds commas and periods based on pauses and patterns. Lawyers speak in long sentences with lists and conditions, so the marks may land in the wrong places. A misplaced comma can change which condition applies to which duty.

causes.title: Legal vocabulary is unusual
causes.text: Case names, Latin phrases, statute references and defined terms are rare in everyday speech. Most general dictation tools do not know your matter. Expect the most errors in the names and terms that matter most, not in the easy words.

causes.title: You speak at thought speed
causes.text: You dictate while you think, so sentences run long and clauses tangle. Long sentences give the recognizer more chances to slip. Short chunks, one paragraph at a time, make each error easier to catch and easier to fix.

causes.title: No review habit
causes.text: Many people skip the read because the draft looks professional. Clean formatting makes errors harder to see, but it does not make them less likely. A written routine forces the read that a polished page tempts you to skip.

fixes.title: Set the built-in Dictation options
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Decide on auto-punctuation and stick with that choice for each matter. Use the blue underlines as your first checklist, and click each one to choose the right alternative. This costs nothing and works on any Mac.

fixes.title: Keep a plain word list for each matter
fixes.text: Start a short note with party names, judges, courts, dates and defined terms. Keep it open while you dictate. Search each term during the first read. The list costs nothing, and it catches the errors that matter most.

fixes.title: Dictate in short chunks
fixes.text: Speak one paragraph, pause, then continue. Use a headset mic in a quiet room. Stop to read back a sentence when it runs long. Short chunks make errors easier to find and easier to fix.

fixes.title: Run the same three-pass check every time
fixes.text: Pass one reads for meaning. Pass two checks facts: names, dates, numbers and negatives against the file. Pass three reads the whole draft aloud. Use the same order every time, so you never skip pass two when a deadline is close.

fixes.title: Track changes and compare versions
fixes.text: Turn on Track Changes in Word before you edit, so a reviewer sees each change. Use Compare in Word to check the final draft against the earlier version. Both features come with Word for Mac, so you do not need a new tool.

fixes.title: Get a second reader inside your firm
fixes.text: Ask a colleague to check the final draft against the file before it goes out. A fresh reader catches what you have stopped seeing after many reads. Keep that reader inside your firm's rules for client data.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Set up the settings and word list
plan.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation and decide on auto-punctuation. Write a short list of party names, judges, courts and defined terms. Add them to your personal dictionary in Lazur if you use it.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Dictate one real draft in short chunks
plan.text: Dictate one paragraph at a time and pause between chunks. Use a headset in a quiet room. Do not edit while you speak. Read each paragraph back once you finish it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Run the three-pass cleanup
plan.text: Pass one reads for meaning. Pass two checks names, dates, numbers and negatives against the file. Pass three reads the whole draft aloud. Write down each error type so you can spot patterns.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Get a second reader
plan.text: Ask a colleague to check the final draft against the source file before it leaves the office. Follow your firm's rules on sharing client material. Keep a short log of what the reader caught.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Keep what works and drop the rest
plan.text: Look at your log after a week. Keep the settings and word list that caught the most errors. Drop any habit that added time without catching anything.
